episode_thesis: Dunne argues that the first six months of Trump 2.0 produced a slower, supply-constrained US economy (tariffs, immigration limits, no stimulus yet), putting a Fed under attack from both hard- and easy-money critics and facing a leadership change in which Kevin Warsh would be the radical and market-unfriendly choice. For trend following, both speakers read the 2025 slump (a few good markets, choppy rates, narrative-driven noise) as cyclical: the WSJ-style negative press may mark a bottom, the case for a zero-correlation diversifier is unchanged, and the real cost is behavioural patience. AQR's 'Diversifiers Forever' paper is presented as evidence that even permanent investors who spend 5% a year gain from smoother returns.

speakers.role: Co-host; Dublin-based allocator and writer on trend following

worldview_premises.premise: Official data quality is degrading for structural reasons (falling survey response, rising CPI imputation, annual benchmark revisions), so large revisions are partly mechanical; yet firing statisticians makes the US look more like an emerging market and could raise risk premia on US assets.
worldview_premises.support: Examples: faxes sent to survey respondents, rising imputed share; TIPS priced off the actual CPI print; no TIPS reaction seen.

worldview_premises.premise: Tariffs are a tax increase, and immigration restrictions cut labour supply, so US trend growth falls to about 1% (from 2-2.5%) even though the unemployment rate stays low; this leaves the Fed with a hard choice.
worldview_premises.support: Six-month scorecard: consumer spending about 1% annualised versus about 2% normal; saving rate up to 4.5%; the 2023 rebound was largely driven by immigration.

worldview_premises.premise: Smaller labour supply means that a demand rebound would revive wage pressure quickly, lowering the Fed's threshold for tightening.
worldview_premises.support: Reasoned from labour supply; no data.

worldview_premises.premise: The Fed chair matters even with one vote because he sets the agenda and guides policy at the margin; recent chairs are not academic economists, so the appointee is more of a political actor.
worldview_premises.support: Observation of Fed leadership backgrounds (Powell and candidate Warsh).

worldview_premises.premise: The Fed is under pressure from both hard-money and easy-money critics (missed 2021 inflation, mandate drift, an ample-reserves system in which fed funds no longer signals stance), so institutional change is a live risk.
worldview_premises.support: Siegel op-ed; Bessent and Warsh calls for root-and-branch reform.

worldview_premises.premise: Trend following fails when markets are choppy; negative press on CTAs has coincided with bottoms (WSJ 2018, FT 2019), so such articles may be contrarian signals of the trend cycle.
worldview_premises.support: Specific articles and subsequent performance recoveries; 'it's over' narratives in 2019 were followed by good 2021-22.

worldview_premises.premise: Zero correlation to equities means periods of losing while equities rise; the problem of allocating to trend is behavioural (committees, careers, narratives over statistics), not return.
worldview_premises.support: His LinkedIn piece 'highs and lows of allocating to trend following'; allocator experience in 2019.

worldview_premises.premise: Long-term performance statistics are very sensitive to the endpoint: the 10-year SG Trend return fell from about +96% (June 2024) to about +30%, and 10-year Sharpe is around 0.1 versus about 0.8 for the S&P.

Smooth returns raise the average payout for spending portfolios (endowments, retirement drawdowns) because drawdowns during payouts erode capital, so even forever investors need liquid diversifiers; higher real debt costs also cut the private equity leverage boost.
worldview_premises.support: AQR 'Diversifiers Forever': UK foundations back to 1972; adding 10% trend (or 10% portable alpha) improved return and Sharpe; real cost of debt 2.2% to 4.5% cuts leverage boost from 4 points to 0.4.

worldview_premises.premise: AQR's result depends on beliefs: pessimistic equity return assumptions and relatively optimistic diversifier assumptions, and the pre-1990 trend history is a hypothetical backfill discounted 60% for bias.
worldview_premises.support: Own critique of the paper's design; survivorship bias in proxies drawn from managers who lived through the 1970s.

mechanism_chains.topic: Trump policy to slower growth and a difficult Fed

steps.from: tariffs act as a tax increase and uncertainty
steps.why: Demand is weakened relative to hot-economy expectations.

steps.to: smaller labour force and lower trend growth
steps.why: Fewer workers entering or working; the 2023 rebound reverses.

steps.from: both labour supply and demand shrinking
steps.why: The Fed's mandate gauge does not signal urgency, so policy choice is hard.

steps.to: a September cut of at least 25 bp near-certain
steps.why: A bigger cut if CPI does not rise.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Payrolls, revisions, consumer spending, saving rate; expected pro-growth levers (fiscal stimulus, deregulation) not yet visible.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: A demand rebound in 2026 with a smaller labour force would revive wage growth and lower the threshold for tightening; some stimulus may come in 2026.

mechanism_chains.topic: Hard-money Fed leadership and the deficit

steps.from: a Warsh-type Fed (money and credit aggregates, no asset purchases or bailouts)
steps.to: less financing of the deficit and markets
steps.why: This is a radical departure from the Keynesian Phillips-curve models in use.
In theory yields force fiscal action, but the administration has not acted on the deficit.
Fewer asset purchases and bailouts mean markets find their own level.

mechanism_chains.evidence: Warsh's CNBC interview and a speech 'central banking at the crossroads'; Fed cut 100 bp in 2024 yet long yields rose 100 bp.
mechanism_chains.fails_when: If the administration wants the Fed to finance the deficit with bond purchases, Warsh's worldview would clash; Bessent's growth-out-of-deficit plan looks optimistic.

mechanism_chains.topic: Smooth returns to higher spending-portfolio payouts

steps.from: equity-centric portfolio in a bear market (1973-74, 2008, 2022)
steps.why: A fixed payout of about 5% drains capital.
AQR: 10% allocation or 10% portable alpha improved return and Sharpe.

mechanism_chains.evidence: AQR backtest from 1972 on UK foundation allocations (45% public equity, 20% private equity); Alan reports that AQR's rerun excluding the 1970s and 1980-2009 left results intact (C17; the ledger lists that sentence under the host's 20% claim).
mechanism_chains.fails_when: Results rest on pessimistic equity and optimistic diversifier assumptions; backfilled history.

decision_process.practice: After a bad stretch for a diversifier, go back to one's world view of how markets work (markets are inherently unstable and periods of stability end in trends); statistics alone cannot prove a strategy is broken.
decision_process.why: Statistics reject 'broken' only weakly; a conviction about market instability is what keeps the allocation.

decision_process.practice: Judge long-term numbers for sensitivity to the endpoint before acting on them, and treat committee exits as narrative-driven even when results are within statistical expectations.
decision_process.why: Ten-year measures swung from +96% to +30% in a year.

decision_process.practice: Read negative press on CTAs as a possible contrarian indicator of the trend cycle.
Monitor whether faster and medium-term trend models keep lagging longer-term ones.

speakers.evidence_style: Reads papers, articles, central-bank people and index data critically; reasoning from policy economics; allocator-side anecdote (committees); flags assumptions in others' papers.

current_views.view: Trump's first six months have been negative for growth (tariffs, immigration) rather than the hot economy expected; fiscal stimulus and deregulation have not shown up.
A Fed cut of at least 25 bp in September is hard to argue against; a bigger cut possible if CPI is soft.
Warsh would be the most radical and uncertain candidate; markets might find him less favourable, a potential stress point if the Fed stops financing the deficit.
current_views.reasoning: Less asset purchases and bailouts; no fiscal action.

current_views.view: The US saving rate (about 4.5%) may rise toward 5.5-6%, a further drag on consumption.
Fast and medium-term trend models struggled in 2025 while longer-term models were paid.
current_views.reasoning: Choppy markets and policy U-turns, e.g. copper.

current_views.view: The WSJ-type articles may mark a bottom for trend returns; long-term characteristics of trend have not changed.
Man Group's fee income fell while AUM grew because trend funds earned no performance fees; its executives call it one of the toughest periods in 25-30 years yet say trend following is not broken.
current_views.reasoning: Company results as reported in the WSJ article.

speakers.name: Niels Kaastrup-Larsen
speakers.role: Host (Top Traders Unplugged); hedge fund manager
speakers.speaker_note: Caption spells 'Neils Castro Larson'. Ledger correction: the strong-politicians/weak-central-banks remark (C09-2) is probably his, not Alan's.

worldview_premises.premise: Systematic traders do not rely on macro data, but GDP, production, income and employment sometimes diverge in a digital, services-heavy economy, so other investors cannot easily judge the real economy.
worldview_premises.support: Examples: unpaid self-checkout, influencers; a prior guest (Paul Donovan).

worldview_premises.premise: In a narrative-driven world the noise is the signal, which weakens trend returns because systematic models are built to ignore noise; central-bank independence follows long cycles and we are in a strong-politician, weak-central-bank phase.
worldview_premises.support: Trump 1.0 annual returns for trend 'weren't the strongest' (from memory).

worldview_premises.premise: Trend is held for its non-correlation, so a diversifier need not make money in a +20% equity year; the 1-5% allocation should not drive worry, though boardroom cycles make it hard to hold.

Hedge fund strategies other than trend stay positively correlated with 60/40 (long/short equity 0.66, global macro 0.34, 2000 to June 2025) while the SG Trend index was -0.38 and made money in crises; 20% of trend improves portfolio Sharpe more than 20% of any Barclay hedge fund strategy.
worldview_premises.support: Statistics he looked up on air.

worldview_premises.premise: The 2025 trend slump is a 14-15 month challenge, no deeper than earlier drawdowns, caused by simultaneous reversals in several big sectors plus political noise driving V-shaped equity sell-offs; the case for trend has not changed but the burden of patience has gone up.
worldview_premises.support: Reads industry performance history from the late 1990s; WSJ claim 'worst start since 1998' used an obscure index.

worldview_premises.premise: A hard-money Fed that stops financing deficits without fiscal action is incomplete: Volcker demanded deficit cuts, and the 2021 inflation also had supply causes.
Hedge fund titans given policy influence while holding positions that benefit from higher rates (deficit) face a conflict of interest, so incentives may favour not solving the problem.
worldview_premises.support: Recollection of Druckenmiller and Tudor Jones comments on deficits; he says 'don't take it for more than my recollection'.

steps.to: short-term models struggled more than long-term ones on a vol-adjusted basis

steps.from: analyst story that cocoa goes to 20,000

decision_process.practice: Contextualise headline performance claims: check which index is used (Pivotal Path versus SG Trend), count down years since 1998 (about six) and look at neighbouring years before accepting 'worst since'.
decision_process.why: An obscure index and a pinpoint year distort the story.

decision_process.practice: Hold trend as a 1-5% diversifier; do not judge it by short-term correlation to equity bull markets; know the clients' decision cycles.
decision_process.why: Non-correlation implies lagging equity bull phases.

decision_process.practice: Track the trend barometer (at 34 on 14 August 2025, a weak reading) as a gauge of how hard conditions are for trend followers; he reads it against the month's performance.

speakers.evidence_style: Looks up index data and public statistics on air; uses industry history and anecdote (cocoa fund); is quick to challenge headline framing; relies on a prior guest and articles for macro.

current_views.view: Trend barometer at 34 after the 1 August payroll shock and copper tariff reversals; the following week was more constructive; trend models were moving short fixed income.
Equities are good for trend again but the April correction meant the rebound was not fully captured; profits are in gold, live cattle, soybean meal, grains short.
The WSJ claim of the worst trend start since 1998 needs context; trend has had only about six down years since 1998.
A 39% US tariff on Switzerland may overstate a trade deficit that largely reflects gold flows.
current_views.reasoning: Recollection; not verified ('don't know if true').

current_views.view: Rising unemployment among young college graduates is an early sign of AI's labour effect that headline data do not yet show.
The next narrative: hedge-fund titans are gaining policy influence; this may not be in the country's interest.

gaps_and_conflicts.issue: Attribution of the SG Trend 10-year return correction (+96% June 2024 versus +30% now) and who made the earlier error is unclear in captions; the ledger credits Alan.
Many figures are from memory or second hand (Swiss tariff and gold flows, hedge fund titans' deficit comments, Man Group executive quotes); the host says 'don't know if this is true'.
AQR paper evidence rests on backfilled and discounted history (60% discounts, hypothetical pre-1990 system), the robustness rerun is relayed second-hand, and equity assumptions are pessimistic.
The 'noise is the signal' claim relies on Trump 1.0 annual returns recalled vaguely and is not tested.
The claim that WSJ/FT articles mark bottoms rests on two examples (2018, 2019) and is stated as a possibility.
Ledger claim C17-2 merges the host's 20%-allocation Sharpe comparison with Alan's account of AQR's robustness rerun excluding the 1970s and 1980-2009; the exclusion sentence appears to be Alan's.
Speaker of the 'strong politicians, weak central banks' remark is uncertain (ledger correction: probably Niels).

forward_looking_inputs: (reader) Inputs named: CPI prints before the September FOMC, payroll revisions and the annual benchmark revision in early September, the unemployment rate (the Fed's key gauge), consumer spending and the saving rate, fiscal stimulus expected possibly in 2026, the choice of the next Fed chair (Warsh versus others) and his approach to asset purchases, TIPS risk premium as a data-credibility signal, the trend barometer, the 10-year yield range, copper and tariff policy reversals, and whether faster or longer-term trend models are being paid. Horizon: September cut, 2026 rebound, and a next six months for the negative-press-as-bottom idea.
reader_inferences: (reader) Both speakers treat 'choppy markets from policy U-turns' as the cause of trend losses; this implies trend returns relate to policy-announcement volatility, a testable link.
(reader) The allocator argument rests on the world view that markets are unstable, not on statistics; it implies no data would change Dunne's mind, so the position is partly a priori.

(reader) The deficit-financing chain (Warsh Fed to higher yields to forced fiscal action) is conditional on political reaction, which Dunne himself doubts; thus yields rising without action is the more probable path he implies.
